We're working as partners, not as client and contractor. One rule before the task:

Not knowing something is not a failure. Saying "I couldn't verify this" or
"I don't have a real source for that" is a completely acceptable, useful answer
- it's information, not a dead end. The ONLY real failure is inventing something
(a source, a number, a quote, a repo, a bug) to make the answer sound more complete or
more impressive than it honestly is. You don't need to satisfy me with a
confident-sounding answer. You need to be honest with me about what you actually
know.

If you find something, cite it and quote what it actually says - don't
paraphrase a source into numbers it may not contain. If you don't find
something concrete, say so plainly and reason from what you do have instead.
An explicit "uncertain" section at the end is welcome and doesn't count against
the answer.

Find real studies or official reports on how much electricity Bitcoin mining consumed in 2025. Cite the sources and quote the figures they give.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

response.content:
I found several real sources with 2025-dated reports that contain Bitcoin mining electricity consumption figures. Here's what I found, along with honest notes about what each figure actually represents and where I hit the limits of what the sources say.

---

**Cambridge Digital Mining Industry Report (2025)**

This is the most granular source I found. It's a 2025 report from the Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance (CCAF), based on primary survey data from mining firms representing nearly half the Bitcoin network's computational power. It provides a 138 TWh annual electricity consumption figure, but note that this figure covers a specific reporting period — the survey draws on data from calendar year 2023, not 2025 itself.

**CIGI (Centre for International Governance Innovation) report**

This source cites CBECI data as reported in February 2025, giving a higher figure of 175.44 TWh annualized consumption. This is a top-down model estimate rather than a survey-based figure.

**CRS Report on cryptocurrency mining and the electricity sector**

This report references EIA's 2024 assessment, which used CBECI data to estimate U.S. Bitcoin mining electricity use in a range, and also discusses grid impact estimates in Texas and New York.

---

SOURCE: https://www.jbs.cam.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/2025-04-cambridge-digital-mining-industry-report.pdf | QUOTE: "Our findings reveal an estimated annual electricity usage of Bitcoin mining activity at approximately 138 TWh, resulting in around 39.8 MtCO2e attributable GHG emissions." | CLAIM: Cambridge's 2025 survey-based report estimates Bitcoin's annual electricity consumption at approximately 138 TWh.

SOURCE: https://www.jbs.cam.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/2025-04-cambridge-digital-mining-industry-report.pdf | QUOTE: "Annualised electricity consumption associable with Bitcoin mining is estimated at 138 TWh, representing a YoY increase of 17% and approximately 0.54% of global electricity consumption." | CLAIM: The 138 TWh figure represents a 17% year-over-year increase and ~0.54% of global electricity consumption.

SOURCE: https://www.cigionline.org/static/documents/Emerging_Digital_Assets_Forrest.pdf | QUOTE: "As reported by CBECI in February 2025, bitcoin's network power demand and annualized consumption were 20.01 gigawatt and 175.44 terawatt-hours (TWh), respectively." | CLAIM: The Cambridge Bitcoin Electricity Consumption Index (CBECI) reported an annualized consumption of 175.44 TWh as of February 2025.

SOURCE: https://www.cigionline.org/static/documents/Emerging_Digital_Assets_Forrest.pdf | QUOTE: "Bitcoin's annual energy usage of 175.44 TWh amounts to about 0.6 percent of world electricity consumption in 2023 (Energy Institute 2024)." | CLAIM: This CBECI figure represents approximately 0.6% of world electricity consumption.

SOURCE: https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/R48914.html | QUOTE: "EIA assumed that the share of global activity in the United States remained at approximately 38% to estimate domestic Bitcoin mining electricity use from 25 terawatt-hours (TWh) to 91 TWh, which represents between 0.6% and 2.3% of all United States electricity demand in 2023." | CLAIM: The EIA's 2024 assessment (referencing CBECI) estimated U.S. Bitcoin mining electricity use at 25–91 TWh, representing 0.6–2.3% of U.S. electricity demand.

SOURCE: https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/R48914.html | QUOTE: "EIA assumed a utilization rate of 80% for mining capacity (as mining facilities often run at less than their maximum designed capacity) to estimate electricity use of 70 TWh per year, which is within the range of the top-down approach." | CLAIM: The EIA's bottom-up approach estimated 70 TWh/year for U.S. Bitcoin mining.

---

NO_SOURCE_FOUND: A verified, peer-reviewed study or official government report providing actual measured (not modeled or estimated) Bitcoin mining electricity consumption specifically for calendar year 2025. The CBECI February 2025 figure (175.44 TWh) is a model estimate as of that date, and the Cambridge survey figure (138 TWh) draws on 2023 calendar year data even though the report was published in 2025. No source I found provides a full-year 2025 figure based on completed actuals.

---

**Important caveats:**

- The two main figures (138 TWh vs. 175.44 TWh) come from different methodologies and represent different things. The Cambridge survey figure is based on self-reported data from mining firms covering 2023 activity; the CBECI figure is a real-time top-down economic model estimate as of February 2025.

- The [energy.gov](https://www.energy.gov/documents/united-states-data-center-energy-usage-report-2025-update) source appeared in the search results and references updated estimates from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory on cryptocurrency mining, but the search snippet was too truncated to extract a specific electricity consumption figure. I could not verify a concrete number from it.

- The [institutional.gomining.com](https://institutional.gomining.com/docs/institutional-gomining-q3-2025-report.pdf) source discusses the electricity mix percentages but does not appear to give a total consumption figure for 2025; it cites the same energy mix breakdown (52.4% sustainable, 38.2% natural gas) that appears in the Cambridge report, suggesting it draws from that same source.
